svg.desc: Banner for a paper on log-concavity of counts of commuting permutations sorted by their number of joint orbits. Left: a spike plot of σ(n)/n, the sum of the divisors of n divided by n, for every n from 1 to 720, computed exactly; the tallest spikes, highlighted, fall on numbers with many small prime factors, and the factorials 4! = 24, 5! = 120 and 6! = 720 are marked, 720 being the highest. A dotted line marks σ(n)/n = 2, the abundant numbers. This factor sits in the one-group count, which is the denominator of the two-group log-concavity ratio. Right: at two groups the ratio tends to zero along factorials, so log-concavity fails in every rank, with certified failures at a 54-digit n for three shuffles and an 845-digit n for four; at three or more groups it holds once n is large, with exact lim inf about 2.52 for three shuffles and three groups, where the elementary bound gave 1.10. Footer: the spikes are exact divisor sums for small n; actual failures occur only at astronomically large n.
svg.text: Where log-concavity breaks: only at two groups
commuting shuffles counted by joint orbits; the two-group ratio divides by a count that spikes with σ(n)/n
sum of divisors ÷ n: the factor in the one-group count
ratio → 0 along n = m!: fails in every rank
first certified failure, 3 shuffles: a 54-digit n
Spikes are exact divisor sums for small n; actual failures occur only at astronomically large n
